title: Suturing a flap laceration
stem: Procedure room. Mr Chan, 58, a construction worker, has a V-shaped flap laceration on his left shin from a metal edge 3 hours ago. Consent has been obtained. Repair it on the skin model.
notes:
Checked against RCEM/BSSH wound care principles, the UKHSA Green Book tetanus chapter (2023 update), and standard suturing technique.

Assess: mechanism, time, contamination, foreign body, tendon/nerve/vessel injury, tetanus status, diabetes/peripheral vascular disease (pretibial wounds in older patients heal poorly — consider steri-strips for thin skin). Prepare: aseptic field, irrigation with saline, local anaesthetic (1% lidocaine, max 3 mg/kg plain or 7 mg/kg with adrenaline; your notes use 4 mg/kg, the US figure), explore, debride non-viable tissue. Flap: the half-buried horizontal mattress (corner) stitch at the tip preserves blood supply; simple interrupted sutures elsewhere (vertical mattress where eversion is needed). 4-0 non-absorbable monofilament on the leg; removal at 10–14 days for the lower leg (7–10 days for other limb sites). Non-adherent dressing. Tetanus: a tetanus-prone wound (soil, manure, delay over 6 hours, devitalised tissue) needs a booster if not fully immunised or last dose over 10 years ago, and immunoglobulin for high-risk wounds in someone not fully immunised (UKHSA) — not simply '>10 years since last dose'.

Your notes cover the procedure, handling of sharps and instruments, and complications, matching this.

steps.label: Prepare
steps.hint: Suture set, sterile gloves and drape, antiseptic, saline, lidocaine, 4-0 nylon, dressing, sharps bin.

opts.t: Suture pack, sterile gloves, drape, chlorhexidine
Normal saline and syringe for irrigation
Non-adherent dressing; sharps bin at hand

opts.r: Multifilament silk carries more infection and tissue reaction; use monofilament.

steps.label: Repair
steps.hint: Neurovascular check, anaesthetise, irrigate, explore, corner stitch at the tip, interrupted sutures, dressing.

opts.t: Check distal neurovascular status; check the flap's colour
Clean the surrounding skin; infiltrate lidocaine from within the wound edges
opts.mark: Local infiltration through the wound edges

opts.t: Test sensation; irrigate with saline under pressure
Explore for foreign bodies and deep injury; trim non-viable tissue
Corner stitch (half-buried horizontal mattress) to anchor the flap tip
opts.mark: Places a corner stitch at the flap tip

opts.t: Simple interrupted sutures 5 mm apart, 5 mm from the edge, needle at 90°, edges everted, knots to one side
Dispose of the needle into the sharps bin; dress
Transfixing stitch straight through the tip of the flap
opts.r: Strangulates the tip's blood supply; use a corner stitch.

opts.t: Pick up the needle with your fingers

steps.label: Aftercare
steps.hint: Tetanus, suture removal time, wound care, infection signs.

opts.t: Tetanus: last dose 15 years ago and a dirty wound → booster (and immunoglobulin if high-risk and not fully immunised)
Remove sutures at 10–14 days (lower leg); keep dry for 48 hours; elevate the leg
opts.mark: Suture removal timing and wound care

opts.t: Return for redness, pus, fever or increasing pain

qs.a: Anchors the tip without strangling it
wrong: Faster closure of the whole wound
Better cosmesis, but only on the face and neck
A surgical incision closed within 6 hours

qs.q: Vertical mattress suture is useful for…
wrong: Inverting the edges of the wound

badge.name: Stitch Master
badge.flavor: Irrigate, explore, corner stitch the tip, everted edges, never touch the needle.

options: Less infection risk and tissue drag
Any wound more than 10 years after the last dose
Through intact skin 5 cm away only
After suturing, into the closed wound

cards.q: Pretibial flap in an elderly patient with thin skin?
options: Leave open to heal by secondary intention
